utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to -- I beg your pardon. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. I guess we got to say good morning to the people in New York. Where are they? Can we see them?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Sacirbey, and to everybody else in New York.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, we can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are all looking at me like they can't hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, we can, Your Honour. Yes, I can. Can you hear us? We are speaking back. We can hear you. We can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Can you hear us, though?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can now hear you. Thank you so much. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, could we have appearances for the day, starting with Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. It's Barney Thomas, Lorna Bolton, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all. Milos Androvic, Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Tina Drolec, Colleen Rohan, Novak Lukic, and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. We go through the ritual, Mr. Sacirbey, just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please have 65 ter 6076 up on the screen which will be tab number 80, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, I note that your lawyer is not in attendance, and I therefore will not be asking you any questions which I believe could potentially impact upon those issues for which your lawyer is to be with you. But could you tell me, please, if you know when your lawyer might be appearing.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that. He is coming in just the next 15 minutes. He is coming from out of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You previously had an opportunity to look at the first seven pages of this particular document that's 65 ter 6076, which were introduced into evidence and have become P2485. What I would like you to do, if you could, please, sir, is take a look at the balance of the documents that are contained within tab 80. And I think it might be more fruitful for you to take a look at them collectively before I ask you any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this tab 80 what we see on the screen here, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just a minute, Your Honour, I'll let you know. Yes, it is. And I don't know if you are getting static, I am. Quite a bit, as a matter of fact. I don't know whether or not the Chamber is experiencing the same thing as I am, it sounds like it's raining rather hard. It sounds like a Hague storm. That occurred as a result of me turning off my microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please turn your microphone off again then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Mr. Guy-Smith, I think I've reviewed the written material rather quickly. There is, of course, numerous supporting material with charts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Exactly. And with regard to that material, is this material that you've had an opportunity to see before today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I believe I've had the opportunity to see the contents, if not necessarily this exact draft. At least some of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say you've had an opportunity to see some of the contents, I take it that, for example, if I were to refer you to those pages that deal with the individual trace analysis report, that is what you are referring to with regard to having had an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't hear you now, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to try something to see if this works or not. Can you hear me now? Mr. Sacirbey, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. I won't do any more of the Verizon commercial again today. Could I please get the assistance -- could I please have some technical assistance, so I'm able to have a conversation with Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good, let's see how this works. I'd like you to take a look at what would be in e-court page number 34 of 73. For your purposes it will be, if you look at the bottom of the pages, it would be 0172-1402, which is Appendix 2 to Annex F, ICF inquiry dated 5 May 1995, trace serial number 2.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date was 5 May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the assessment of the trace, you'll note that there it says that the assessment of the trace is unexplained; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the lion's share of the appendices that support the seven-page conclusion that you discussed previously with Ms. Bolton, would it be fair to say, and I'm trying to do this rapidly, that the lion's share of them indicate that the trace -- the assessment of the trace is unexplained, that in those incidents that were scientifically examined by the commission, the issue of border crossing through scientific determination was unexplained?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly see there's several of those explanations. I cannot make a quick assessment as to what is the dominant assessment of the trace. I see several different explanations. But certainly unexplained is on more than one and quite a few in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard -- and I thank you for that answer. And with regard to another explanation that's given with regard to the issue of assessment of trace, there is the following determination. For example, if we could go to page 48 of the same document in e-court, which will be 0172-1416. It's trace serial number 15. The assessment of the trace there is "insufficient data for analysis;" correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's at least one such that I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you were to look at the next page, which would be page 49 which is trace serial number 16, you see the same entry, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to make sure I get to the right page.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I am ahead of myself then. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you be willing to accept that between the entries of unexplained and insufficient data for analysis that covers the lion's share of those documents that you have just reviewed, with regard to the question --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems like a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the question of unexplained border crossings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along with insufficient data for further analysis, that seems to be by far the lion's share.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would move the admission of the remainder of this particular exhibit which was previously given the number of P2485 as Defendant's next in order, or it may make more sense to just make this one entire exhibit. I don't know what works best for the Chamber or for the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like what is best for the process is for them to be made one big exhibit, part of 2485.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have P201 up as the next document I'd like to discuss with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Can we have the tab number, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is Prosecution tab, this is Resolution 752, and I'll get it for you in second. I believe, if I'm not mistaken, it's tab number 6 in the first Prosecution binder. In the 1992 -- in the 1992 Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if I could direct you to paragraph 4 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we speaking of a UN resolution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We are. We are speaking of Resolution --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resolution 752?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent. As I understand your testimony, it is your position that at the time the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was incumbent upon them to do one of two things under this resolution; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it's your position that the resolution required that they either turn the arms over to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as one solution; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Or they deliver the arms that were to be left, if at all, to the international community; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I would say there's obviously a third element here which is to actually take the weapons out of the country along with the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to clarify that because I had not heard you give that particular response when you were testifying on direct with regard to this matter. That there was a third potential opportunity. Now, the thing that you are -- if I understand, the matter that you were objecting to was the JNA leaving the territory. By any chance could you tell us when that was, when the JNA actually left?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I think you know my testimony, I do not believe that they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is impossible to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your opinion is that all that happened was there was a transfer -- I'm sorry, I'm being told I need to do something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith, the interpreters are complaining that it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Interpreter, what is impossible to work with?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was too much noise for us to hear either the witness or Mr. Guy-Smith. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I'm speaking at this point, can all the interpreters hear me? Yes? I'm okay all the way around? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I seem to hear you directly, Mr. Guy-Smith, and not via the earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me try here. Do you hear me through your earphones, or do you hear me directly, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you hear me here, or do you hear me directly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doesn't seem to be a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't know exactly whether or not the matter is being recorded or not recorded. I don't know how to best to proceed, because I don't know what the technical issues are as to whether or not -- if everybody can hear me, and Mr. Sacirbey can hear me, I am assuming we have at least a written record of these proceedings. I don't know whether we have an oral record of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe proceed, and if everybody else hears you, then I'll see how to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I understand your testimony correctly, one, you believe that there was never a withdrawal of the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you have any awareness of the killing of the young soldiers leaving the Marshal Tito Barracks in June of 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt my friend's question, but certainly at this point what we have heard of it, I will be having a relevance objection to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there is testimony -- well, I'll wait. We've previously heard testimony from at least one witness with regard to the withdrawal of the JNA at or about June 5th, it may been before Ms. Bolton's entry into the case, in which there was, and I use the word killing as opposed to massacre, which is the word that had been used previously. The massacre of some young soldiers who were leaving the Marshal Tito Barracks pursuant to the agreement that the JNA was to withdraw from the region. And my question is whether or not he has any awareness of that particular matter and whether or not that would impact at all with regard to his opinion concerning the withdrawal of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't know what evidence my friend is referring to. It may have predated my time. I, again, am not clear on what the relevance is to -- of the massacre of the young soldiers to these proceedings. I am in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you don't make any objection then Your Honour doesn't have you in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I continue to object on the basis of relevancy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have my question in mind, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I believe you mentioned a date and you mentioned the phrase massacre. I am generally aware of the events. I am not sure that either the date or the reference to massacre is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I had initially --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, that's been -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I had initially used the word -- excuse me, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to also highlight to the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me Mr. Sacirbey. There's no question pending. I initially used the word killing, and my question is are you, based upon the answer you've just given, aware of an incident involving young JNA soldiers departing from the Marshal Tito Barracks in the month of June as a result of the agreement that the JNA would withdraw from the area and during the time that they withdrew they were killed? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware -- I am aware of JNA units withdrawing from the Marshal Tito Barracks in Sarajevo. Again I question the time-frame that you are highlighting here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by that you question the month of June?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. And I'm also -- I'm influenced by recent events where Serbia has raised its own potential prosecution of individuals involved with that particular incident. So I'm obviously influenced by the discussion of that in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that is a recent influence that you have then?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's been ongoing for about a month, month and a half now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you've answered most of my question, but you have not answered the issue of whether or not you were aware of these young soldiers being killed or not in the process of withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all you characterise young soldiers, I am aware that in fact there were battles involved; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it's your testimony as you sit here that there were battles that occurred during the time that these soldiers were withdrawing from the Marshal Tito Barracks; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my testimony that when they were leaving Sarajevo, this occurred; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not my question, sir. You used the word "battles." Because you used the word battles, we need to have an understanding about that. Is it your testimony that there were battles that occurred during the time that these soldiers were withdrawing from the Marshal Tito Barracks, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you to now go back into your memory as opposed to dealing with those things that may have influenced you in the recent press. Do you recall that there was an agreement between the president of Bosnia and Panic, and that would have been I believe Zivota Panic concerning the withdrawal of JNA troops from Sarajevo and specifically from the Marshal Tito Barracks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that subsequent to this agreement whilst these troops were withdrawing, that's when these battles occurred?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure of the time-frame, but I knew in fact that there was fighting involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, when you say you knew there was fighting involved, are you attributing the battles to this particular incident, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. And most of my knowledge was obtained over subsequent time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say most of your knowledge was obtained over subsequent time-frame, from whence did you obtain that knowledge? Was it obtained from your president, from your military commanders or from the press?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, much of it was also obtained from UN officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your president, did you obtain the information from your president with regard to the issue of these battles that you have alleged occurred?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: A limited -- limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say limited, what do you mean by that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My most extensive knowledge of this issue came up during a visit to Zagreb, Croatia, in the spring of 1993, when I was supposed to go to Srebrenica with the UN delegation. I spoke with then the UN military and the UN head civilian commander and this matter came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you spoke with the UN military and UN civil head commander, who did you speak with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Nambiar in part, and also the civilian commander and his name always escapes me, but he was replaced by Mr. Akashi subsequent to that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is it my understanding it's your testimony that you received the information from these two individuals with regard to the issue of their being battles that occurred at the time that these soldiers were withdrawing pursuant to the agreement that existed between your president and Zivota Panic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We haven't covered the issue of your military. Did you receive any information from your military with regard to that same issue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the press. Did you receive information from the press which characterised this situation? And by that I'm talking about the same withdrawal as being a battle?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely I did. But my greatest source of information and influence is on the basis of those conversations in Zagreb in the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How many conversations did you have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at least one conversation, and I remember it was a UN headquarters. It probably lasted for half an hour to an hour because it related to other events around that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue concerning the weapons that were left behind, you were aware of the fact that at that time there was a contention that those weapons did not belong to Bosnia-Herzegovina as you've asserted; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Mr. Guy-Smith, let me correct the Court, I do remember that gentleman's name, it was Cedric Thornberry, who was the chief UN civilian commander, the other individual I had those conversations with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey, we have frozen video now. While we are waiting, for your information, Ms. Bolton, I'm going to be going to the articles that I had sent over there which had come from the green light report which had heretofore been illegible in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Will they be tabbed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there are a series of them, but most of them are going to be from, I believe it's going to be tab 82. There will be a series of them, and there will be another place where they are, I'll get them to you as we go along. I can assure you they are all in e-court. The first one will be, for purposes of everybody's edification, 65 ter 4564, which is an article dated August 23rd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we connected? Can you hear us, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Sacirbey? Am I good with everybody?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I'm good? Thank you. You might recall that we, the last time we met, we were discussing a series of newspaper articles which you candidly said, and I understand why you could not read, they were illegible, they were part of the Iran green light report. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to at this point in time go through a number of those articles with you. The first one is 65 ter 4564. I'm sorry, that's 1D03 65 ter 4564. I said it backwards I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't have a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It does not have a P number, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the screen is frozen again. We can hear you just fine, but the screen is frozen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, it looks like we are going to have to take a break and see if the technicians can help us because we just can't go on like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a short break. When we are reconnected, you will be called. Thank you. --- Break taken at 2.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Testing, testing, Mr. Sacirbey, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I can, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. If we could have 1D03-4564 available on screen and also available to Mr. Sacirbey, which I believe is the first document in the packet that was delivered sometime a week or so ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, you've discussed with us that you read a number of news periodicals. I take it one of the news periodicals you read, not only privately but also in your capacity as the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina was the "New York Times," was it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is one of the articles that was contained in the document that we were discussing a couple of weeks ago, that being the Senate subcommittee report concerning various arms being moved into, among other places, Bosnia-Herzegovina, called the Iran green light report. With regard to the first document in front of you, dated August 23rd, 1992, I'd like to know first of all whether or not you are familiar with this newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the second page of the article in which there is the following discussion. It says "Government Admits Effort. Ejup Ganic vice-president of Bosnia and Herzegovina acknowledged in an interview that his government is trying to raise money in the Middle East for weapons purchases." Do you have that in front in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the statement made, is that something that was discussed while you were at the United Nations building with some of your colleagues concerning the violation of Resolution 713?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you are speaking of violation of Resolution 713. We certainly did discuss assistance to provide the necessary resources for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to defends itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I understand the euphemism you are using here, sir. What I'm asking you is really very simple. I appreciate the fact that as far as you were concerned, 713 did not apply to Bosnia-Herzegovina. You've made that quite clear. What I'm now driving at and trying to understand is whether or not there was a discussion with other members at the you United Nations concerning the fact that the purchase of weapons would be on its face a violation of Resolution 713, which would have been -- something would have been a concern to you as the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina because you would have had to take a position on this issue. So my question is with regard to the information contained in this article, is that something that you discussed with your colleagues at the United Nations, irrespective of your position with regard to whether or not you had the right to purchase weapons or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very accurate, the issue of the purchase of weapons did not come up. The issue of weapons or other necessary resources coming in to defend Bosnia did come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could turn to the bottom of that page where it says: "Help from Arab Relief Groups." "There are also persistent rumours that arms dealers from the Middle East are at work on behalf of Bosnia and Herzegovina, out-gunned military forces. General Armin Pohara?" Do you know who that is, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He is not one of the individuals that you had contact with in terms of what was going on, on the ground during your tenure as ambassador; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. "... confirmed that 180 mujahedeen from the Middle East have joined the Bosnian ranks." Do I take it that it was your position that not only were you entitled to purchase arms in order to defends yourself, but you also were entitled to have foreign nationals, by that I mean individuals from outside of your country, come into your country in your defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of foreign fighters did come up. And one can classify them into two categories. One is mercenaries, the other one would be so-called volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by volunteers you mean --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, we took the view at the UN mission --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took the view at the UN mission that any foreign forces coming to Bosnia were not welcome. And we frankly discouraged them at least from the UN mission. As to their legality, I never took a position on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to -- with regard to the information that's contained in this particular article, one with which you are familiar, did you have conversation with your president or any military leaders back at home concerning the fact that you were having foreign nationals fighting for you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was that also a conversation that you had with some of your colleagues at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is this also a matter that you had some concern about, and by concern I mean when you had mentioned to us the other day that there was, I believe, leakage in your government, that this kind of information is the kind of information that would be of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, again, sorry, I'm not getting any sound. Oops. Sorry to interrupt, again I'm not seeing the relevance of this line of question to any of the issues that were raised during either examination-in-chief, Your Honour, or the issues that are before this Tribunal in terms of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Notice. Common discussion between all that were going -- common discussion between all during the period of time that the issues that are germane to these proceedings were being discussed, the resolutions, the violations of the resolutions, how they were being interpreted, and general understanding of what information was available upon which all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Notice to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Notice to who?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Overruled. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, could the Chamber kindly informed me as to when we are going to stop because I'm happy to go as long as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see. Can we just -- I'm not quite sure how much longer we can still go on the tape, but may I suggest that you go on, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely until somebody tells me to stop, very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have my last question in mind with regard to your concern about leakage within the government?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and actually, this is not a point of concern that I had regarding leakage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please now have 1D03-4569. Which would be, I believe, the next document. Once again this is a "New York Times" article, dated September 10th, 1992. Iran said to sends arms to Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, what should the fate of ID --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can I please have that admitted into evidence as Defendant's next in order, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. ID03-4564 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit D136. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at the document, sir, the article?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good. First of all, I'd like to understand something if I could. Is it your position that arms being sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina could be sent in any fashion whatsoever including as relief for humanitarian aid, and that was legitimate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly if something was labelled as a humanitarian mission, then we owed it, I think, to the institution that was providing the humanitarian assistance to make sure that the humanitarian assistance did in fact come through and not something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So then I take it that by the answer you've given, you would say that if in fact you -- by you I'm saying Bosnia-Herzegovina were receiving arms under another guise, that that would be illegitimate; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly one of the concerns that I had regarding the arms embargo is that it could in fact corrupt a whole system of delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact you know that it did corrupt the whole system of delivery. And let's take a look at this article.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the first document: "'Evidence of military support by an Islamic country to the Muslim-dominated government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian officials have intercepted a planeload of Iranian arms and personnel,' western officials said today." Going to the second paragraph: "Its ostensible mission was to deliver relief supplies for overland delivery to Bosnia and Herzegovina. But when the plane was inspected, Croatian officials discovered 4.000 guns, more than a million rounds of ammunition, and 20 to 40 Iranians huddled in the back." You would agree with me, sir, would you not, that those items are not humanitarian or relief aid?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the story is accurate, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is this a story that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the story, but I must say that I was never aware of any Iranians that were fighting on the side of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, were you aware of some 20 to 40 Iranians huddled in the back of a plane trying to sneak into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly am not on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Continuing with the article: "'While there have been unconfirmed reports that Islamic countries have been providing military aid to Bosnian Muslims, the seizure of the Iranian shipment represents the first tangible evidence,' Bush Administration officials say." You were discussing this issue of the arms embargo with Bush Administration officials, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You, as a matter of fact, discussed this very incident with him, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly, but I don't recall the discussion if that's what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you telling us that this particular discussion escapes your memory at this time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect it specifically. One did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I please have this moved into evidence Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit D137. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 1B03-4610 [sic], I believe this document -- this is a publication from the "Los Angeles Times."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have that document in front of you, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Can we have the tab number, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely. It's tab number 84. Sorry, Mr. Registrar. That would be in the new batch.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is this a document that you are familiar with, this particular publication, this particular article, I should say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm familiar with the article, although of course I'm familiar with the publication and the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the subject matter, referring your attention to the second paragraph which says: "The shipment was one of the most brazen efforts yet to circumvent a year old UN arms embargo in the region. It has intensified concern that Iran and other nations could fuel an already explosive civil war by giving new firepower to the Bosnian Muslims who are battling Serbian forces for control of the former Yugoslav republic." Now, is that a matter that was discussed between you and your colleagues at the United Nations? And by that I'm talking about the particular concern here, the shipment could fuel an already explosive civil war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly again the issue of weapons shipment was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you were told, were you not, as it says, for example, in this article, going down three paragraphs: "'We don't need more weapons in Bosnia,' one US official said. 'More arms are not going to help reduce the level of tension and violence and bloodshed.'" You were told that, were you not, by concerned individuals and your colleagues at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly something of a similar sentiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "certainly something of a similar sentiment," I take it what you mean --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's whole issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it what you mean by that --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it what you mean by that is that you were told in no uncertain terms that more weapons would exacerbate the situation and that your decision, and by that I mean Bosnia-Herzegovina's decision, to obtain weapons outside of the embargo was inappropriate and ill-advised?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The words inappropriate and ill-advised depends on whose perspective you were looking at. Bosnia was already badly out-gunned, and in fact much of its population was already on the run, and cosmopolitan areas were under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So your position was being a member state of the United Nations at that point in time that you would interpret 713 in a manner that you deemed most appropriate for what you believed to be the benefit of your country; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were under aggression; there was genocide; and there were already weapons in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, Mr. Sacirbey, Mr. Sacirbey, please listen to my question. Your position was being a member state of the United Nations at that point in time that you would interpret 713 in a manner that you deemed most appropriate for what you believed to be the benefit of your country; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we believed most legal and consistent with our obligation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I please have that as Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit D138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the issue of relief, and by that I mean relief supplies being in these shipments, what was actually going on, and you were aware of the fact that it was going on, is that arms were being sent to your country under the guise of humanitarian aid, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of. Not at least of specific situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I take it by that, that you have difficulty, then, with the accuracy of the article that we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the "Los Angeles Times" article?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought the question to the witness was about his knowledge. And now my friend has asked him a question about the accuracy of an article. I don't think the witness is in a position to comment on the accuracy of the article. He'd had no firsthand knowledge. He has told us he hadn't read the article until today. I just don't think it's appropriate for him to be commending on whether the article is or isn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not a problem, I'll withdraw the question. I can do this in a entirely different way and would be more than happy to. Could we have 1D03 -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm just trying to move as quick as I can because I'm worried about breakdown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 1D03-4574. Which I believe, Mr. Registrar, should be the third document in the first package. This is an article from the "Washington Times."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I have that, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is this one of the articles that you were reading during the period of time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading the first few lines, I'm at least aware of some of the contents of this, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the second paragraph, it says: "'We'd seen various aid shipments go in independent of the UN and had raised our concerns with the Croatian government and said you might want to check these things out,' said a senior US official who asked not to be identified." Now, with regard to the issue of various aid shipments, were you aware of the fact that your country was receiving, and I use the term euphemistically, various aid shipments which in fact turned out to be arms in violation of Resolution 713?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was the case, at best I know only as isolated incidents. My biggest concern, frankly, at that time was to what extent Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled at borders. And we were concerned, at least I was concerned, about in fact what could be coming through those borders in the form of either illegitimate supplies or men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the -- with regard to the answer you've just given, it says, and I want to make sure we are on the same page, I was concerned about in fact what could be coming in through those borders in the form of either, is it illegitimate supplies, or is it -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's the term I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. The transcript said something slightly different. I just wanted to double-check. Now with regard to your concern about there being illegitimate supplies, I take it this is something that you voiced to your president or other members of your government while you were in New York, working on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, we would have discussions on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the diplomatic dance you were going through at the time you had to deal with the reality on the ground as well as make sure that you kept a certain level of diplomatic, shall I say, validity while you were at the United Nations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that's correct. My focus was on two things. First of all, in any way undermining the flow of humanitarian supplies which I certainly perceived as being essential, so any sort of corruption of that system would be very troubling. And certainly, number 2, I would be concerned about the flow of men into the country, which would very much undermine what I understood to be Bosnian's ideological goal in terms of preserving a secular multi-ethnic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that what you did because of those concerns when you received the information like the information we are discussing here because of the potential impact it would have, the negative impact it would have, that you wrote to your government and said, Stop this from happening. Do not let this occur. Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly had those types of discussions with my government; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you write to them about it? Did you memorialize it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the first point would be try to verify if there was any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, my question to you is, Did you memorialise these concerns that you had discussions about in the same fashion that you've memorialised so many other things?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did memorialise it, I don't have the specific recollection of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Curious.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, if my friend could refrain from making inappropriate sarcastic remarks on the record, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise. Tab 41, please, 1D03-0792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to do with this one first?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have it moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit D139. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'm reviewing that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a letter that you wrote on 18th of May, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It actually reflects a letter from President Izetbegovic, yes. It introduces it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a letter that was distributed; correct? In the general distribution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a letter --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it has been.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is a letter that indicates that the current mandate -- and I'm going to the second full paragraph. It says: "We believe that the current mandate of the United Nations forces in our republic is inadequate." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph, once again, there's a discussion about voiding the arms embargo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the mandate that your president is indicating is inadequate, are you referring to the mandate coupled with the rules of engagement that existed at that time for self-defence by UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The view was that in fact there needed to be a clear mandate to confront attacks upon the republic and, of course, its citizens and territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say there needed to be a clear mandate, it was your position, was it not, that UNPROFOR at that time should be acting in a, what I would call, a proactive fashion as opposed to a peacekeeping defensive fashion; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I think the word you would want to say peacemaking versus peacekeeping. There was no peace to keep at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, we certainly agree about that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: So obviously you need to make the peace to keep it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And it was your position that what should occur - when I say your, I'm talking about your position as the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina - is that UNPROFOR should engage in active military activity in order to make peace; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, depending on the environment. If we are talking about delivery of humanitarian assistance, they should ensure that is delivered. If we are talking about attacks upon the country and particularly the population, then in fact those attacks could be -- should be confronted. We are now talking about that critical phase in time when the safe areas resolution was being adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And are you limiting your answers to those two areas as being what your position was concerning what the UNPROFOR mandate should have been?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all sincerity, that's a difficult qualification. I think what we are saying is there is no peace to keep. Before there can be a peace to keep, you must make sure that in fact there is a peace, and of course at the same time you must make sure that the civilian population, the population as a whole is in fact adequately fed and taken care of and protected from attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could that be marked as Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So marked. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit D140. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could please have tab 47, Mr. Registrar. That's 1D03-0806.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was comprised of a number of different member states including Russia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This letter is a letter in which you are indicating, and by that I mean your president is indicating that you do not approve of the arrival of additional Russian troops to Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the conditions that existed, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the conditions that existed was apparently there was, as I understand the letter, looking at the first paragraph, there was some disapproval of the manner in which the Russian soldiers behaved on their arrival to Sarajevo which raised discontent among the Sarajevo citizens and harmed the reputation of the United States mission; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe United Nations mission you were referring to, not United States, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in this letter, you are attributing -- I am sorry, by that I mean President Izetbegovic is attributing behaviours to the Russian UNPROFOR troops that they were in support to the aggressor; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that would -- the aggressor being the troops of General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have this marked as Defendant's next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit D141. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have tab number 48. 1D03-0808.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'm familiar with the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a letter that you penned; correct? That is not a letter that comes from your president; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I believe did come from several sources, including Sarajevo, but that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in this letter you are, if I'm not mistaken, looking at the very -- the second to last paragraph before you asked for it to be circulated: "It appears this is arrangement may be rescinded under pressure, nonetheless I'm saddened to inform you that the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by this act and other more recent behaviour of certain United Nations related personnel..." And I take it there so we're clear you are referring to Mr. Akashi; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very honest with you, I'm not sure who the reference to is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We'll get to that then.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We'll get to that; it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I do remember the incident, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Your Honour, again I'm not clear on the relevance of this document to my friend's line of questioning, particularly what particular individuals Bosnia-Herzegovina had an issue with or, for example, on the last document, the behaviour of Russian peacekeepers. Again I don't see how either of those issues relate to live issues in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm still trying to find out where you were reading, Mr. Guy-Smith. Maybe if I can see that, I can see whether there's any relevance or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. In order for you ultimately to make an assessment with regard to our client's mens rea, you are going to be looking at a series of documents and publications that all went into various determinations that were made. And the totality of the picture is something that I believe the Chamber is going to need in order to determine what was done, why things were done, why things were not done, and what the positions were. And clearly, clearly, the kinds of diplomatic give-and-take that was occurring at the United Nations is something that is of import to your ultimate determination. We've heard again and again and again and again about the resolutions that were passed and the about the statements that were made by various members of either the General Assembly or the Security Council with regard to various issues. This is as critical and as much a part of what we are talking about as that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I was asking you where you were reading from this document so that I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It appears, I'm looking at the second to last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which starts with "it appears this ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "It appears that this arrangement may be rescinded under pressure," yes. And it goes on which is -- I had indicated that I thought it could be Mr. Akashi, but it goes on: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has lost all confidence in these individual's actions to promote the United Nations mandate and an overall peace settlement in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could respond to my friends's comments. Again I don't see any link in terms of the mens rea with this document. The issue of the mens rea is in part depending on whether on 7-1 or 7-3 would be, for example, did he have notice of the fact that there were allegations of crimes on the part of the Bosnian Serb army? That has nothing to do with the contents of this letter, the contents of the previous letter. So any relationship, as far as I can see, the mens rea is non-existent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I understand Mr. Guy-Smith to be saying is that what his client did he did in response to some of the things that are being said here, and that therefore he wants the mens rea of his client to be looked at against the background of what had come to his knowledge about the activities of the opposite number in the war zone. Now, that's how I understand him. Am I misunderstanding you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You are not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For that reason, then we will not allow your objection. I'm sorry, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the statement that is made there, when you indicate that you have lost all confidence in these individuals' actions, was that a matter that was discussed, first of all, amongst your colleagues at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, there was an assault ongoing upon Gorazde and weapons were being moved from Sarajevo in furtherance of that assault, and we saw this as a direct help to the Serbian forces by allowing them to take weapons out of the exclusion zone in Sarajevo and move them upon an assault on another exclusion zone which was the safe area of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, Mr. Sacirbey, once again I'd appreciate if you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before he does so, can I just get clarity, Mr. Guy-Smith. When you say discussed with your colleagues, who do you mean? His office mates in the Bosnia-Herzegovina mission or in the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've been using that as form for in the United Nations, Your Honour. And I'll be clearer. And I understand your question; I'll be clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I'll tell you now what I find a little putting -- it's like you are putting the cart before the horse, because my understanding of this letter is that he is tabling it before the United Nations and saying, Let's discuss. He didn't discuss it before he wrote the letter. He is asking it to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that's the case or not; I'm trying to find that out. You may well be right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Having His Honour's concern in mind, first of all, is this a letter in which you were requesting that the matter be discussed by members of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... read that last paragraph, the one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm referring -- would you like me to read that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm referring to: "It appears this is arrangement may be rescinded under pressure, nonetheless I'm saddened to inform you the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by this act and other more recent behaviour of certain United Nations related personnel in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has lost all confidence in these individuals' actions to promote the United Nations mandate and an overall peace settlement in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was referring to the very last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "May I ask for your kind assistance in circulating this letter as a document of the Security Council." And was that done, sir, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a result of that being done, was there a discussion with regard to the concerns that you have raised in the second to last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, in the context of the elaboration I gave a couple of answers earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have this as Defendant's next in order then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit D142. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue contained in the second to last paragraph of Exhibit D142, all confidence in these individuals' actions, if we could please have tab 42. That will be for you, which will be 1D03-0794.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter of 6 May 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. That, I believe, would be the day after the letter we were just discussing, which was the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could just beg my friend's indulgence. The tab 42 in my binder that was provided doesn't match, and I'm just trying to find this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It would be 1D03-0794.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll just try to follow it on e-court, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, first of all, this document was circulated; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in this document, once again, I'm going back to, for a moment, the individual that was being discussed on May 5th. Looking at the letter, it says: "The Secretary-General special representative for the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Yasushi Akashi has destroyed all the confidence which our government has placed in him and which was the basis for any form of cooperation." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Goes on to say that: "Methods have been witnessed," in paragraph 2, "that can only be described as counter-productive in handling the critical issues of war and peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next paragraph goes directly to the matter that you were raising concerning Gorazde in which you take the position that Mr. Akashi acted in obvious contradiction with relevant Security Council resolutions and decisions of NATO Council; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, particularly Resolution 752 and 757 requiring that Serbian heavy weapons either be placed in the hands of the international community or be surrendered to the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this case, those weapons in fact were allowed to move freely through the exclusion zone and in fact toward an attack on another safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What you are referring to is the Serbian tanks that were being complained about in the previous exhibit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the position that Bosnia-Herzegovina took as it related to the United Nations representative, you took the position that Mr. Akashi has practically placed himself on the side of the aggressor. "I am convinced that very few well-meaning individuals including his closest associates can comprehend or explain Mr. Akashi's actions." And then the letter concludes with the following paragraph which is: "I'm obliged to inform you that for the above-stated reasons, the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina can no longer cooperate with Mr. Akashi." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you took this position that your government would no longer cooperate with Mr. Akashi, I take it by that, that you felt you were no longer bound by considerations that existed under the various resolutions that we have been referring to; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Independent of 713, of course.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. That's actually not correct. Let me make sure I clarify why it's not correct. Number one, I certainly did not take that position. And second of all, I am not referring to -- this letter does not refer to UN Security Council resolutions. But in fact as my explanation before, in fact we are concerned that Resolution 752 and 757 is being violated by allowing weapons to be employed which were previously either in exclusion zones or under international control.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, so we are clear, when you say I certainly did not take that position, are you saying that in your capacity as the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina you did not take the position that is stated in this letter by your president, President Izetbegovic, is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I should be clear on that. The point is, this is a view that President Izetbegovic took, and of course that view at some point in time did at least change to some degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from that which is something we may well get to, what I'm asking, the point in time that you circulated this letter, are you telling us that you said, I'm circulating this letter on behalf of my president, my colleagues on the United Nations Security Council, but this is not my position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I'm saying that in fact this is a position taken by President Izetbegovic, and it certainly did not reflect our position on UN Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the issue of -- with regard to the issue of UN Security Council resolutions, you say on page 42 at line 1: "And second of all, I'm not referring to -- this letter does not refer to UN Security Council resolutions." Well, my question to you is this: As a matter of fact, as I read the letter, it very specifically discusses UN Security Council resolutions in paragraph 3 where it says: "His conduct and decisions regarding the crisis around Gorazde are, in our opinion, in obvious contradiction with the relevant Security Council resolutions and decisions of the NATO Council." Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've I'm consistent on that point, Mr. Guy-Smith, I am not sure where you believe the inconsistency exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you make assumptions, sir. You make assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can I have this admitted as the Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit D143. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have 1D03-4576, which will be I believe, Mr. Registrar, tab number 4 in the original packet of newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I'm reviewing the article, and I'm familiar with its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say you are familiar with its contents, let's see if we can figure out in terms of time a couple of different issues. First of all, I take it we would agree that the article comes from the "Washington Post," and its date is the 13th of May, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's discussing an Iranian air force transport plane loaded with 60 tonnes of explosives and other raw materials for weapons production, landed in Zagreb last week as part of a deal between Croatia and Bosnia to renew military cooperation against the Serbs, western and Bosnian sources say. And I take it some of those Bosnian sources that asserted this in this May 13th article are individuals who you spoke with or had information from concerning this particular transport plane?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who those Bosnian sources are, but I'm familiar again with the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next thing is: "The May 4th arrival," next paragraph, "of the Boeing 747 cargo plane in Croatia's capital marked a conspicuous violation of the arms embargo imposed by the UN Security Council on Yugoslavia and its former republics in September 1991." Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the information that is contained here, you were aware of the fact that on May 4th, the day before the letter was written on May 5th, that there had been a shipment of explosives and other raw materials for weapons productions that were seized for the benefit of your country, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to personally I was aware?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to whether or not you had that information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I certainly don't recall getting that information for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge -- to your knowledge was your president who wrote the letter on May 5th which you had circulated at the United Nations aware of this particular seizure?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to --
