utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the next paragraph it says: "Velayati," who I understand to be the Iranian foreign minister "presented Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic with a check for $1 million and a chit for 10.000 tons of diesel fuel. Izetbegovic responded with what appeared to be a thinly-veiled statement of thanks for Iran's military support." Now, these were matters which you were aware of, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly aware of this article. I don't remember having discussed this particular event with President Izetbegovic, but I'm certainly aware of the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was this article and the information contained in this article a matter of conversation with you and your colleagues at the United Nations General Assembly or Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if the article was, but again, the subject matter was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the subject matter being the fact that you were continuing to receive, by that I mean Bosnia-Herzegovina, was continuing to receive armaments that caused concern in the international community in relation to the prohibitions of Resolution 713; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without the characterisations, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the characterisation being the prohibition of 713 which you dispute; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the word "concern."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Concern. You do not believe -- it's your testimony that the shipment of armaments in May of 1994 was not of concern to the international community?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying first of all, as you've pointed out that it was not a violation, and the word concern I think reflects only one element of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, sir -- so you and I disagree there. I contend it was a violation; I am acknowledging that you -- that it's your position that it was not. I have no doubt about what Resolution 713 says, as far as I'm concerned, but I'm not the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I think in both of our instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could turn to -- if we could turn to the third page of this article. I'm sorry, it would be the second page:

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go back a page, Mr. Registrar. Thank you so much. And go down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, starting with the paragraph that says: "Cooperation was strengthened further in late April when Croatian prime minister Nikica Valentic led a delegation to Iran to take Iran and sign an agreement with Iran to facilitate the delivery of 'humanitarian and technical assistance to the Bosnian people.'" Were you --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm just trying to find the -- oh, I see it. It's at the top of page 3 here. I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Top of page 3 of the hard copy. That's correct. Now, were you privy to this particular agreement to which you were the beneficiary -- I'm sorry, to which your country was the beneficiary, that's the delivery of "humanitarian and technical assistance to the Bosnian people"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of it but I was not privy to the specific terms of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, and with regard to technical assistance, I take it that what we were referring to was armaments, are we not, among other things, weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did understand is as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, looking at the very last paragraph, it says, and I quote: "'This is the first weapons-related convoy from the highest level since the war began,' said a Bosnian military source. 'It's a groundbreaker. We are hoping for more.'"

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, is that particular quote attributed to somebody who you know, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of. I frankly don't know who it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the attitude that's contained therein, is that, is that in fact the position that you were taking at the United Nations concerning the importation of arms to Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994, in May of 1994? That you were hoping for more?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly don't -- I'm not aware of who made this quote. And second of all, I think I would be reading too much into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you endorse that position in your capacities as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina in May of 1994, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that in fact additional assistance was needed for Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend itself, its country, territory and population, I would endorse it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could that be marked as Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit D144. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 1D03457 -- 4579. Page 4, please. Which I believe will be, Mr. Registrar, I believe that it's going to be tab number 5 in the first packet of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, what I'm referring to is page number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry I missed that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'm just wondering, is it one of these articles -- or is it from the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's one of the articles, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm referring to page number 4 which starts off with "Iran said to violate embargo." And I'm specifically referring to not the issue of Iran but the second paragraph which indicates: "The Bosnian army also received" -- you are going to have to go to page 4, Mr. Sacirbey, otherwise we won't be working with each other.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The second paragraph which says: "'The Bosnian army also received a large shipment of anti-tank rockets delivered to Croatia by a Brazilian ship,' said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity." Were you aware of the fact that your country was receiving anti-rockets sent through a Brazilian ship?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To that specific question, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this particular newspaper article, which is also dated the 13th of -- sorry, not also dated -- yes, it's also dated the 13th of May, are you familiar with any information concerning Brazilian ships smuggling weapons for the benefit of your country?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I specifically recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am, of course, aware of the need for anti-tank weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Different issue. With regard to the next paragraph, which is: "Four convoys carried the rockets and explosives to central critical Bosnia in the last few days after Bosnian Croats took a one-third cut of arms, he said." Is that something that you were privy to, a deal between your county and the Bosnian Croats, whereby you would split up the weapons that were being smuggled in so that you could use them for those purposes you deemed appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of agreements between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. As to any other arrangement, it may have fallen into the agreements with the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to those agreements that you've just told us you were aware of, those agreements were something that you made common knowledge of to the international community of the United Nations, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you speak of me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm speaking about you in your capacity as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that your country made it known that you and Croatia were involved in a deal whereby you would split up arms that is would come into your country, you would get some of them and Croatia would get some of them.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I did that personally, although I'm quite certain that that information was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, when you say available, is this the kind of information that you published, as you've published other information, or is this information that you are telling us you believe was out on the grape-vine?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter statement is more accurate than the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Considering the position that you took, Mr. Sacirbey, with regard to your right to self-defence, can you explain to the Chamber why you did not at that time make public to the world that you were involved inside arms deals whereby you would be obtaining weapons for the benefit of your nation which you believed to be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Guy-Smith, most countries do not make public information regarding receipt or even manufacture of weapons. We certainly took the view that in fact weapons were entitled to come; that's correct on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you take the view that you were entitled thereby to have weapons come from another nation such as -- or another nation state such as Croatia, who is also subject to 713, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and whose territory at that time was also occupied, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it's the your position that not only Bosnia-Herzegovina but also Croatia, to the extent it was occupied, also was not bounds by the strictures of 713; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was primarily for Croatia to make that determination but I think your conclusion is more accurate than not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was your position, sir, is what I'm asking. I'm not asking what Croatia did, that was your position. That Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That Croatia too --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. That Croatia as well --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Guy-Smith, first Croatia would have to -- Mr. Guy-Smith, first of all, Croatia would have to take its own position -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that, Mr. Sacirbey. I'm interested in your position as a diplomat in front of an international body fighting for your country where you have a side agreement with another nation state in order to obtain weapons that have been deemed illegal under 713.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the cart comes ahead of the horse here, Mr. Guy-Smith. Croatia, first, has to make that determination, and only then could I act upon that determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once Croatia has made that determination, then, Mr. Sacirbey, I take it, it was your position that this certainly was not information that you wanted out in the public, and by that I mean that you would publicly acknowledge that you were doing this, this being illegally bringing weapons into the country?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. In fact, we did acknowledge that weapons were coming in and other necessary resources for defence. We took that position firmly on by 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so we are clear because I certainly don't -- my understanding is you are aware of the information that is contained within this particular newspaper article, but you are not aware of the article itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You took me all the way to the back, so I haven't read the beginning of it. I think I'm actually -- I think I am aware of the article, but I was reading right from the back so it didn't jog my memory, but, yes, I am aware of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well, could I have that then marked as Defendant's next no order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit D145. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honours, but I do note the time. We've now being going for another hour and 25 minutes or so. For both my sake and perhaps the sake of the witness, I wonder if we could have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. I've been trying to do mental arithmetic how to divide the remaining time. I was coming to that, but now that you are asking before I even get my answer. We'll take a break and come back at 10 past 5:00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This will be tab number 8 in the original packet. It's 1D03-4589. This is a "Washington Times" article dated June 2nd, 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I have that in front of me, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The article starts out indicating that: "Up to 400 Iranian Revolutionary Guards have been sent to Bosnia to organise terrorist groups among Muslims in the region, according to United States intelligence sources." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next paragraph discusses the arrival of the guards and shipments of arms and explosives in May; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And we were earlier discussing before the break the seizure of shipments of explosives as well as the discovery of Iranian guards in the month of May, 1994; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was something that you were aware of, as I understood your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I would like to do is I'd like to turn to what I believe is your page 2. And it seems that information is now being received that expands the fighters, the international fighters from those of being only from Iran to including now fighters from Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Syria. And I am going to ask you a series -- I'm gonna talk about the article for a moment and ask you a series of questions rather than talk about each one of these things. The next paragraph indicates: "'The Saudi government has supplied several hundred million dollars' worth of arms to the Bosnian Muslims,' US officials said."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next paragraph: "The activities of the Iranian Revolutionary Guards in Bosnian could complicate efforts to reach a peace settlement between Bosnian Serbs and Muslims." I want to stop here for a moment, with regard to the information that is contained within this article dated June 2nd, 1994, in your capacity as the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, first of all, were you aware of the fact that fighters from Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Syria were in Bosnia as reported in this article?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of fighters from other countries including Middle East, that is correct. As well as countries like Romania, Greece, but also from the Middle East; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say from the Middle East, so we are clear, I take it that you were indicating that you were aware that they were fighters, from Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Syria, and I take it from your answer other member states of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be more precise, they would have been referred to as Arab origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Once again we seem to be --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the -- sorry go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We seem to be talking at somewhat cross purposes. I understand that you were aware that there were fighters from the Middle East. Were you aware of the fact that there were fighters being supplied to Bosnia-Herzegovina from Egypt, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are saying fighters being supplied, which seems to emphasise that, in fact, these fighters were being somehow channelled through a regular means. I am aware that there were a lot of fighters of Muslim background, particularly many Arabs, and many of them came from western Europe as well as the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the fighters that came that are mentioned in this particular paragraph, and I understand your particular concern, that you do not want to answer the question to say that these were state sanctioned fighters, my question is, Were you aware that there were fighters who came from Egypt?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm only aware that fighters came of Arab origin or Muslim origin from many places, the Middle East as well as western Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So then your answer would be you do not have specific information that fighters came from Egypt; correct? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take the same would be true for Saudi Arabia, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I'm -- it seems very likely that they came from those countries, but I don't have any specific name to associate or any specific group to associate with those countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to Syria, I take it you would give the same answer, which is that you do not have any specific information that there were fighters that came from Syria who were fighting in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the assertion made here, that there were fighters from the Middle East who were coming to Bosnia and that the Saudi government had supplied several hundred million dollars worth of arms to the Bosnian Muslims, this was a matter that was of concern to you as the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina in representing the interest of that country before the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that there were foreign fighters on any quote/unquote side. Or to the extent they were particularly mercenaries, that would be a real concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Above and beyond that, you a specific concern, because such reportage that there were quote, and I'm using the term in a generic sense now, following your lead, that there were Muslim fighters, was defining the problem in a way that you specifically did not want the problem defined, and by that I mean along ethnic lines; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Armed with this information, Mr. Sacirbey, is this a matter that you raised with your colleagues in the United Nations in these discussions you had on the record and off the record, that they were not to be concerned about the fact that there were Muslim fighters and Muslim assets and Muslim money being given to Bosnia to help in your war effort?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were not to be concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I would use the word that they were not to be concerned. These were matters of certainly consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say they were matters of consideration, as a matter of fact, they were more than matters of consideration, they were matters of some great moment, because the presence of these assets and these individuals in Bosnia was furthering, according to some, the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the presence of these people could in fact further what you were just speaking of earlier, which is the notion that this was a religious conflict and that in fact it was just a pure civil war. In fact, I never saw it as either a religious conflict or as a civil war. And obviously the motivation for these individuals coming to Bosnia could be very different than the motivation of the Bosnian citizens and soldiers who were just defending their country, in effect defending themselves, and of course defending the territory, and defending against genocide. I think there were in fact potentially two counter-purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One of the things that you objected to repeatedly, if I'm not mistaken, and we heard it in your direct evidence, was when you were identified as being a Muslim nation or a Muslim side; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So with regard to this particular issue, is this an issue that you attempted, and by that I mean, the informations contained here that you attempted to diminish in your capacity as an ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina? And by diminish, I'm referring to discussions had with people at the United Nations, your colleagues at the United Nations, of various member states, to be very clear.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's -- I'm not sure that's accurate. Certainly, I did attempt to discuss this material with President Izetbegovic and others who I had contacts with in Bosnia. Addressed its concern at least from the perspective of Bosnia's ideological and other positions at the United Nations. And to the extent that it did come up at the United Nations, I am not sure I would dwell on it, but I'm not sure I would be evasive about it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the manner in which you presented your arguments in front of the United Nations Security Council and to the General Assembly, you made it very clear that there was a Bosnian side, did you not? A Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is not clear to me. I think you -- is it a two-part question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm getting at is this, Mr. Sacirbey. You very clearly identified your perception of who the various players were in this conflict. One of the players in the conflict --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One of the players in the conflict was the Bosnian Serb side, as far as you were concerned; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you recall my testimony, I referred to it as the Serbian side in almost every communication. I think there are some exceptions to that. Or Pale Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you consistently rejected the notion or the perception or the identification of a Muslim Bosnian side, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Except in one instance, and that is to the extent that Muslims were identified as targets for genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. But Muslims as being identified as individuals who were fighting on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was something you rejected.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not -- that was not something as I viewed favouring the cause of Bosnia-Herzegovina or its, obviously, definition in the future as a multi-ethnic pluralistic state of all its citizens; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say it's something that you did not view as favouring the cause of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's a fact that you diminished in public, the extent to which --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The extent to which Bosnia-Herzegovina was receiving aid and assistance from a particular group, and by that I mean the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's accurate. I think you can receive aid from Muslims without identifying yourself as somehow being part of a greater Muslim cause or Jihad, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sure that may be the case, sir, but with regard to the concerns that were being voiced, if we might, and I refer you to the same article that you are looking at -- and I refer you to the same article you are looking at, if you go down --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One after the indication, the activities the Iranian Revolutionary Guard in Bosnia could complicate efforts, if you go down 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 paragraphs where Mr. Katzman is talking, and he says, "they don't are have to be that fervor," Mr. Katzman said of the recruits sought by the guards. "The guards are like a virus, they get into a country and replicate themselves leaving a militia behind."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are asking me to comment on this overall article, first of all I do not believe there were 400 Iranian Revolutionary Guards in Bosnia, nor do I believe that they were fighters. And seconds of all, there was always a fundamental contradiction between the -- if you would, the Shiite Muslim Iranian Revolutionary Guard and the Sunni Muslims. That contradiction existed throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, I think that you and I may, at another point in time, have a conversation over the difference between Sunni and Shiite Muslims, but I don't think now is necessarily the time or the place, because what I'm dealing with is the perception here, the perception that now we have voiced by Mr. Katzman, a Middle East specialist with a Congressional Research Service which is found in the same article, discussing the dilemma of the Revolutionary Guards on your soil.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And how would you like me to comment on that. I'm sorry. I do read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question is to you, this is a matter that you attempted to diminish and to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you getting instruction?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I was listening. I was waiting to hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if you are getting instruction or not. I heard another voice, so --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- I thought you might be getting instruction.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Whether this was something that you were avoiding in your capacity as the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina to diminish the Muslim issue.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not trying to diminish the issue of whether or not Bosnia was receiving assistance from Muslims or Muslim states. I was trying to in fact present a Bosnia in the context of one that was not committed to a Muslim state but in fact committed to secular pluralistic state. I hope I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You are doing the best you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can we have that marked as Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just I assume my friend, as with the previous exhibits, is proffering it not for truth of its contents but for a state of mind, since the witness has agreed he does not agree with the accuracy of the contents of this article, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Don't mind that at all, not on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The document is then admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit D146. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it we are referring to 456, correct, the last exhibit? Okay. Fine. Can we please have 4592.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does it also start with ID03?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. That would be, I believe, this would be number 9, Mr. Registrar, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that's an article dated the 24th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. "Iranian weapons sent via Croatia aid to Muslims get US wink"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like you to look at the very bottom of this article, where it says: "Pentagon officials are concerned the Iranian arms, while helping Muslims defends themselves, complicate peace efforts, which appear to be foundering due to widespread violations of a June 10th truce agreement."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Actually, at that time it seemed that is the truth was most effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At that time it seemed that the truth was most effective, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the middle of that summer in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do I take it, then, with regard to the statement made here concerning there being widespread violations of that agreement, is that something that you take issue with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember my direct testimony, I believe I was asked what was the status of the truth in the summer of 1994, and I think I indicated that it was probably at its most effective in terms of at least the civilian population and what was happening to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to turn to the next page of this article. And I'd like to go down 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 paragraphs to the paragraph which starts with "Kenneth Katzman ,"I believe the gentleman we were speaking about in the last article, "a specialist on Iran with the Congressional Research Service, said Iran has offered to send 10.000 troops to Bosnia as part of a UN force, but the world body does not want them there." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now is that something that was a matter of discussion within the halls either formally or informally at the United Nations, that Iran had --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Iran --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That Iran had offered to send 10.000 troops to Bosnia at a time when the truce was holding, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Iran in fact had offered to send peacekeepers. The number and the times spanned the range of this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you use the term "peacekeepers" --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only in the context of UN peacekeepers that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you use the term "peacekeepers," is it is your testimony that the 10.000 troops that Iran offered to send were going to be sent through the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now, with regard to the issue of the lifting of the arms embargo, something that you were a great proponent of, if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would like you to go down further in the article where it says: "On Capitol Hill, defence officials from Britain, France, Spain, and Denmark testified before the Senate Armed Services Committee yesterday that a unilateral lifting of the arms embargo against Bosnia by the United States would intensify the conflict." I continue --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "'We believe that the lifting of the arms embargo would have the effect of pouring gasoline on fire and mean an all-out war,' said Danish undersecretary for Defence Anders Troldborg." Mr. Troldborg appeared along with Jean Claude Mallet, the director of strategic policy at the French Defence ministry; General Juan Martinez Ezparza, a deputy undersecretary at the Spanish defence ministry; and Major-General Rupert Smith, director of strategic policy at the British Defence ministry? Now my first question to you with regard to part of the article is you were aware, were you not, that there were hearings in front of the United States Senate arms services committee in June concerning the lifting of the arms embargo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is actually something that we actually discussed the other day with regard -- and I'm asking you the question, with regard to the private conversation that you had with Mr. Holbrooke to back off of Senator Dole; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And just to refresh all of our recollection, Mr. Holbrooke told you that if you backed off pushing the United States Senate for lifting of the arms embargo, that you would get arms by other means; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he put it, from any source including Iran.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now, with regard to this statement here made by Danish undersecretary for defence Anders Troldborg concerning pouring gasoline and fire and mean an all-out war, could you tell us, please, what was your position on the cessation of hostilities agreement as it related to lifting of the embargo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was positive.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the cessation of hostilities, we were certainly positive because it provided the Bosnian citizens with certainly some greater security as well as further assistance. I must point out again, though, that this comment here, I'm not sure what anyone believes Bosnia had been undergoing for the previous two plus years, if it was not an all-out war. It was not only an attack on the country from one end to the other, but in fact the civilian population had been targeted and as I have said --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand your position there.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand your position there. And you've said it the same way they vote in Chicago early and often, and I understand your position. But with regard to this particular concern being voiced by one of the members -- a representative of one of the members of the United Nations that would have the effects of pouring gasoline on the fire, did you take that in consideration when you were pushing for a lifting of this embargo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the position that you took was in the face of such a statement that it was your position that the embargo should be lifted; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was actually our position, if in fact the international community was not capable of suffocating the war, that in fact the Bosnian government and its people should be allowed to defend themselves. Clearly there was not either a will, perhaps maybe there was not a means, but certainly there was not a will suffocate that war, put out the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to turn to the next page of this document, if you could, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the last paragraphs, it says: "Meanwhile, leaders of the United States, Russia, and Europe are expected to endorse a peace plan dividing up Bosnia at an economic summit meeting next month as senior administration officials said."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that what we have on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour. The page breaks are different, so we are going to have to go back a page. It will be the very last paragraph. And if we could now go on to the next page after everyone has had an opportunity to look at that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "'The plan calls for giving Muslims and Croats 51 per cent of Bosnian territory, while Bosnian Serbs would get 49 per cent. The Serbs currently control about 72 per cent of Bosnia. The Bosnian government has reacted negatively to the plan and will eventually resort to military action to obtain more territory by force rather than through negotiations,' US officials said."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that statement is very inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, let's talk about this plan. The plan that calls for giving about 51 per cent of Bosnian territory to Muslims and Croats and 49 per cent to the Serbs. Now, is that a plan that you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who was the author of that plan, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Contact Group, which consisted of five countries as well as the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to -- with regard to the plan itself, is it your position that this is a plan that was endorsed by Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and the plan also -- this article seems to imply that we are talking about a partition of Bosnia. In fact it was only an internal --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There was only an -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no partition ever -- there was no partition that was proposed by this plan. In fact it was only an internal delineation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: An internal deviation or -- Mr. Sacirbey, hold on.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Delineation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Delineation is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to have it this marked as Defendant's next in order with an understanding, once again, because Mr. Sacirbey has taken issue with certain aspects of it, and I think specifically with "the Bosnian government has reacted negatively to the plan," that particular statement is not being offered for the truth of the matters -- contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document should be given Exhibit D147. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have -- this would be tab 82 in the new batch, which would be 1D03-6495. July 2nd article from Reuters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While it's coming, Mr. Guy-Smith, are we likely to finish with this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think so. But we certainly will not take all of tomorrow, I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, this article deals with tonnes of military equipment are landing at a tiny air strip on the island of Krk, and the weapons are taken by road or boat for eventual delivery in Bosnia. Is this part of the route by which your country was receiving arms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you again asking for personal knowledge at the time or?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this moment I'm asking for personal knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not personally aware of this, no. I was aware of, obviously, all the reports of shipments coming in from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware -- referring to the same article again: "United Nations cannot stop the flights, even though it knows the arms are bound for Bosnian Muslims, because Croatia is outside the scope of the arms embargo ... There is nothing we can do except watch these arms being delivered," it quoted United States spokesman Paul Risley as saying. Did you ever speak to Mr. Risley about this issue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You know who Mr. Risley is though?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it escapes me right now, I must admit, although the name sounds familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the next paragraph: "Arms are being flown to Croatia and Slovenia by private companies, some of them British, lured by promises of big cash payouts. Some of the supplies appear to be coming from Ukraine and Iran..." Well, in your capacity as the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you aware of the fact that private British companies were engaged in merchandising the weapons of war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say not specifically, is this something that you had -- is this general knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly was aware that there were many institutions from several countries, and it would not surprise me that many of them would come from non -- traditionally non-Muslim countries, including Western Europe and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I take it we could agree that British -- British company would be a European -- would be a company in a European nation which is non-Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we can agree on that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we can also agree on the fact that the United Kingdom is a member state of the United Nations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have this as Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit D148. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to weapons that you -- your country was receiving, you knew, did you not, that you were getting weapons including the Red Arrow 8s from the People's Liberation Army of China, which are guided missiles; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that point, no, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you were aware, were you not, that your country was receiving RPG22 anti-rockets that were made in Russia, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that anti-tank weapons were a very important element of the defence, and I assumed they were being received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And for the first one you said specifically, and by that I'm referring to the latest wire-guided missiles. Were you aware of the fact during your tenure as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina that your country was receiving missiles from China?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware in the same capacity that your country was receiving RPG22 anti-rockets that were made in Russia? And that may go back to the discussion we had before with regard to the Russian diplomats that you met in the hallways of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not specifically aware of any such designated weapon. I'm only aware of anti-tank weapons having been received by Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And of the anti-tank weapons that you are aware of, are you aware of their genesis, since apparently you are not aware of their specific type, are you aware that Bosnia-Herzegovina received weapons from both China and Russia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that weapons did come from the former Soviet block.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That takes care of one of the two. What about China, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I answered that I really wasn't aware, or maybe it just slips me, but I don't think I was aware of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Tab 50, please, which is 1D03-0816.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a letter, I believe, that you authored which you asked to be circulated in the Security Council on the 18th of August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the issue of -- with regard to the issue of the truce agreement that we were talking about before, perhaps you can be of some assistance. Looking at paragraph 2, it says: "The 8 June 1994 and 12 July 1994 cease-fire agreement has expired without being renewed."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the negotiations regarding the Contact Group plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which in fact was presented in Geneva by the Contact Group at the US embassy, I was actually present at that meeting. And Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted this plan; the Serbian side rejected it. And obviously at that time the status quo on the ground was Bosnian city is still besieged and intermittent fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. Now, with regard to what you've just said, you said the Serbian side rejected it, right, that's what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at paragraph 3 here, and you were quite specific with regard to who rejected this plan, were you not, what you said was in your letter --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- "the Republican Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina accepted the Contact Group peace plan. The Karadzic forces have rejected the plan, and have demanded terms and conditions that are totally inconsistent with the territorial, constitutional, and human rights standards envisioned by the Contact Group's plan. The Karadzic forces, in fact, have effectively proposed the status quo as their basis for a political settlement and therefore would favour a freezing of the current situation." Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is the mouth from which the rejection was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, that's what you wrote, sir; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this was unacceptable to you at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this letter, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, within the context of this letter, you go on to say: "The government and the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are undertaking measures entirely consistent with the terms and spirit of the Contact Group's peace plan. Any attempts to cite the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina explicitly or implicitly as violating a cease-fire, A, are factually incorrect because there is no longer a cease-fire agreement in place ..." And I want to stop there for a minute. And go to the first paragraph of this letter, sir, in which you say: "Upon the instructions of my government, I would like to clarify a recent matter that has been a source of confusion in the deliberations of the Security Council."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What are you claiming was the source of confusion at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the specific incident, but I can only surmise that it had to do with --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you can't recall, I'm not asking you to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- reports of -- no, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Going to the bottom of page 1, you indicate: "The government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina could not be blamed for interpreting any Security Council statements that are inconsistent with the Contact Group peace plan and associated course of action as being a rejection of that peace plan and consequent course of action." Now, with regard to the statement that you made there -- and perhaps we should go to the next page so that you have your full paragraph, which is: "This would be --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- "especially tragic and indefensible, since four members of the Contact Group are also permanent members of the Security Council." When you say on the first page that you could not be blamed for interpreting any Security Council statements, are you referring to resolutions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so because we are speaking of statements coming either informal or formal from the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you referring to any presidential notes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be the case. I just don't specifically recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this language, interpreting any Security Council's statements, would it be fair to say -- and I'm asking for your assistance here, would it be fair to say that what you are discussing here are the oral statements and opinions made by some member during a Security Council meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't recall. Obviously, I remember what the motive is and what the purpose is; I just don't recall what triggered it, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have this letter as Defendant's next in order then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The letter is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit D149. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go to -- it's going to be number 11 in the first package, Mr. Registrar, which is 1D03-4597.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like you to go down on the very first page and see whether -- whether or not you recall this: First of all, so we are clear, and I do apologise to the Chamber, this is an article dated September 4th, 1994, from the "Washington Times."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The second paragraph says: "The Bosnian army has nearly completed a buildup of 200.000 troops and asked the Iranian government, through its embassy in Zagreb Croatia, to provide the military support as part of the next weapons shipment from Iran, according to sources." And then I would like to drop down 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 paragraphs to where it says: "Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic has said recently that lifting the embargo is not necessary because of his country's successful military buildup." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I don't agree with several paragraphs in this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm only asking you about these couple for the moment. Moving on to the next page --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Moving on to the next page: "Officials have said weapons originated in sites including Iran," which we've talked about before, "Iraq, and Lebanon. And the circuitous delivery routes have been used to avoid tracking by western intelligence agencies. "Still the shipments have been followed from the Middle East through," and now we have two new countries, "Malaysia and turkey and into Croatia." First of all, before we go my further, to your knowledge, is Turkey a member state of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what about Malaysia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what about Lebanon?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In your capacity as an ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you aware of the fact that both Malaysia and Turkey had committed troops to work with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the information that's contained in the paragraph that we have spoken about first of all, which is the Bosnian army has nearly completed a buildup of 200.000 troops, had you been informed by your president or your military that such was the case by September 4th, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That in fact Bosnia had nearly 200.000 troops under its command at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you made aware of the fact by your president that lifting of the embargo was not necessary because of your country's successful military buildup?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that statement is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even its attribution to President Izetbegovic. Actually, to be complete, President Izetbegovic did make a somewhat similar statement before the UN General Assembly after the discussion that I cited with Mr. Holbrooke. But I do not -- I do not believe that this particular time and this particular reference is accurate. And also the first paragraph speaks of a major offensive against the town of Gorazde. Well, at least it's sloppy writing because Gorazde in fact was under the control of the Bosnian government. So how can you have an offensive led by the Bosnian government against the town that it holds?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Sacirbey, with regard to the issue of the troop buildup, are you in a position to tell us what the troop strength was in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Region by region, no. Region by region, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was that information that was given to you in your capacity as the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina during your tenure at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been, but I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question: I believe it's going to be page 2 of the same document. It says -- and I'm going down eight paragraphs, it says: "'The Bosnian Muslims have launched numerous grounds attack using special tactics that have given them advantages over the better-armed Serbs,' the officer said. 'They have shown a great ability to move on the ground, to move at night, very innovative.' The officer said the tactics do not reflects Russian or Iranian training but appeared to have been developed by the Bosnian Muslims themselves." Do you agree with that particular assertion made in this article?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, without specifically knowing what the tactics that they are referring to, I think in fact there was of course a need for greater innovation and courage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, is this something -- is this something that you discussed with your president, that in face of --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That in face of the kinds of weapons, that you had to come up with, innovative tactics, and in fact you were successful in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent, but, frankly, I think we were more successful in stemming the tide rather than reversing it. I think in fact there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, my question really is, is this something that you agree with this particular statement contained in this article?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My friend this last few questions just seems to be by asking for the witness's opinions on various subjects, the current subject being military tactics. He is not a specialist or expert in military tactics. His opinions on any matter, really, are of absolutely no import to the Tribunal, and I object on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well ... I'll move on based upon the assertion just made by Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess by that you are saying you accept the objection, and therefore you'll move away from --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I accept the objection based upon her analysis of what she says in her objection. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this specific issue. This specific document. If I could have -- and I believe it's going to be tab 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would move its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit D150.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, just with respect to that last exhibit, I take it again since the witness took exception to great amount of the contents of the document that that will just be noted on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you accept that, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It is admitted for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have tab 52, which is going to be 1D03-0822.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at the document, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 17th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise, I mispronounced your name, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 17th of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. This is a four-page document, which I believe is a letter that was written by you that you asked to have circulated as part of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me. It's a long letter, but I'm prepared for you to ask whatever question you feel is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to start off with the assertion that you make that there is now a new mandate which you call a rogue mandate attributed to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as I understand your objections, your objections are that this rogue mandate, as you call it, gives the Bosnian Serbs a military advantage over Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's best summarised by the last paragraph in the first page. It appears that UNPROFOR had adopted the Bosnian Serb view that the siege of Sarajevo and status of its civilian population as hostages were legitimate military countermeasures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to -- with regard to this particular position that you've taken, could you tell us, if you recall, who was the head of UNPROFOR at this time in October of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was still General Rose. I think it's still a little time before General Rupert Smith would come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And I know that you have a very definite view about General Rose which we may get to, but --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I do about General Rupert Smith, and the views are quite contradictory as to those two individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I'm well aware of that. With regard to this issue here concerning that UNPROFOR has adopted the Bosnian Serb view of the siege of Sarajevo, is it my understanding that when you wrote this letter, what you were suggesting and what you believed at the time was that UNPROFOR was, I use this term, which I think you'll understand, was pitching for the Bosnian Serbs by virtue of the manner in which General Rose was acting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a pretty sharp characterisation. I think UNPROFOR was taking a position of not only neutrality, but favouring the status quo, which in fact I think would very much further the Bosnian Serb position, in particular in their rejection of the Contact Group peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you help us here on page -- it's page 2 in the hard copy, and I'm not sure it's going to be page 2 in the electronic copy, but I'll let the Court know in a moment. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go down to paragraph number 3, you state: "To justify in morally and legally flawed policy more effectively, it would also be appropriate to delegitimize the status and objectives of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, therefore, must be projected as being more or less on the same moral and legal level of the 'Bosnian Serbs.' For this reason, while certain UNPROFOR officials are conspicuously silent in their criticism with respect to numerous opportunities offered by the actions of the Bosnian Serbs, they have," going on to the next page, "been all too eager to find blame, real or fabricated, with respect to the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the matter was one of reprisal. The army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not engage in any reprisals, while in fact there were many documented events and would continue to be of reprisals against UN forces by the Serbian military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the certain UNPROFOR officials who were conspicuously silent in their criticism here, are you attributing this silence to the likes of General Rose?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe at that time I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey. Yes, Madam Bolton, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, again this entire questioning with respect to this document, the views of this witness with respect to other persons in this case, General Rose, I don't see the relevance. Again it's his opinion on --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It might be something if somebody else penned the document, but this is his document. These are his thoughts, his words, and this is something that was published to the United Nations Security Council. So I think we find ourselves in a slightly different position than we've been in before. If my -- if my opponent is taking the position that Mr. Sacirbey's opinions are of no consequence whatsoever in any respect whether he penned the document or as held forth here on a particular subject or not, then I have to reconsider my examination. If that's the position that the Prosecution is taking. That Mr. Sacirbey's opinions in terms of things that he says himself are of no consequence, of no moment, and have no weight with regard to the Chamber's determination of any of the matters that are before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I never fall into the trap of speaking in absolutes. I can indicate that with respect to the opinion -- my friend is asking a question here, it seems to be, that calls for Mr. Sacirbey's personal opinion. With respect to this calling for the witness's personal opinion, my view, it's prohibited under the guide-lines that we've adopted where opinions are generally limited to expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To the extent that Mr. Sacirbey is the author of this document, don't you see the question as seeking a clarification of what he meant when he said -- when he wrote what he wrote?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Not if it doesn't have some relevance beyond -- what is the relevance of what he wrote?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what the relevance is, but the point of the matter is that your objection is based on the fact that your opposite member is seeking opinion evidence from the witness. And I'm saying if this is a document written by the witness himself, isn't that seeking clarification of what he actually meant so that maybe at a later stage he is able to say, Well, the man wrote this, and I asked him what he meant by this, and this is what he said he meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, I should have been clearer in my objection. It's based part on the fact that he is calling for an opinion. But it's also based on the fact that he is calling for an opinion on an issue that has no relevance in and of itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber has sort of ruled to admit these documents simply because of the explanation that was given that they go to notice to Mr. Perisic of what he knew and how he reacted to what he knew. To that extent, we still would not agree with your objection on that ground, but to the extent that what you call opinion evidence sounds to me to be seeking a clarification of what the man meant when he wrote what he wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to what you wrote, Mr. Sacirbey, could you kindly explain to the Chamber, first of all, with regard to the certain UNPROFOR officials who were conspicuously silent in their criticism, who you were referring to in your letter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be fair to say that one of them would have been General Rose; the other one would have been Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You go on in your letter to say, and this will be on the next page, sir. At the very bottom paragraph: "Once again we wish to express our appreciation to the overwhelming majority," and you continue. Thank you. You say here: "Nonetheless, unless corrective steps are undertaken urgently, the overall United Nations mandated actions within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be subverted and become consumed by the consequences of an unauthorised mandate. Sustaining the unacceptable status quo is not the same as preserving the neutrality of UNPROFOR, in fact, quite the opposite. Those responsible for acting outside," next page, please, "and in contradiction to Security Council resolutions must be brought into line or appropriately addressed. "For our part, the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will continue to maximise cooperation with UNPROFOR and other mandated efforts. Similarly, those who act in contravention to Security Council mandates cannot continue to enjoy the privileges and legal status associated with service in furtherance of United Nations mandates." Now, my question here to you, sir, is, as I understand it, you are asking in this letter for, not to put too blunt a point on it, for the removal of General Rose, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you read the paragraph yourself. The first point is to bring him in line with the Security Council resolutions. I think paragraph 4 here, and it's an extensive paragraph, addresses the corrective measures we would like to see. To the extent that these individuals or commanders are unable to live up to their mandate as provided by the Security Council, then the Security Council should consider taking further steps including removing them potentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've used the plural of them, so I want to be fair here to you and certainly don't want to misstate anything. When you say "them," am I correct in my understanding that this letter includes not only General Rose but also Mr. Akashi as being the individuals you are concerned as being outside of acting appropriately?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter is oblique purposely because, of course, I cannot make a direct determination as to who is responsible. But you are asking me for my opinion before, and my personal opinion was with respect to Mr. Akashi and General Rose. Whether upon further examination, the Security Council would agree with that conclusion, and whether the facts would actually bear that out, of course, remain to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, I'll like this marked as Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This becomes Exhibit D151. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And now, with regard to what you've just said which is a relatively strong position, I take it that this is something that you discussed with members of the Security Council informally and formally, did you not? And by that I mean, you identified both General Rose and Mr. Akashi as being individuals who, in your opinion, were engaged in a rogue mandate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally by identifying them, I'm not sure of that. Informally, yes. I don't recall any situation where -- I certainly had references to some direct elements of their performance and how they in fact undertook their mandate. But again, I think this letter stands on its own, and it is intentionally oblique as to naming individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Sacirbey. My screen has stopped. There's no typing, there's no movement of my screen. Half your answer was not typed; the entire answer is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm suffering the same dilemma, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Might be a technical problem we are having somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, we are entirely good at this end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Should we take a five, ten minute break? Or do you want to hold -- whatever you want to do, Judge. I'm happy to do whatever you want to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to make sure first that we can capture your question and the answer to it, if that's possible. If not, maybe we might ask you to re-state the question. But first of all we got to find out what is the reason for this. The stenographer says hers is working properly, so at least we've got the record with her, but we don't have it here. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I have the same experience, this monitor is working, and this monitor is not working. I don't know why that would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, the one that is working is the one that we up here -- or at least me who is computer illiterate. I use that for exhibits, not for transcript, because otherwise I'm not able to pull out my exhibits on my own side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I was going to say that's the same problem I have. I can't watch the witness and the exhibit and follow the transcript. So I would ask that we correct this problem before we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton and I are in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, fine. We take the agreement between the two parties that this problem be resolved, and given the length of time we've been sitting, I think we might take the break for the day and come back tomorrow at that point in time in the afternoon at quarter past 2.00. Let me just make sure that Mr. Sacirbey hears me. Mr. Sacirbey, we have a technical problem. It's late in the day. We are going to take a break and come back tomorrow in the afternoon again, morning for you. The warning stands, no discussions until you are excused from the witness-stand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honour. Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of July, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.29 p.m.
